Q5709.L1t: Monopoly is a board game in which players move small metal tokens around the board to buy properties.
Q5709.L2t: Hasbro has changed the Monopoly token lineup several times, sometimes through public fan votes that retired older pieces.
Q5709.L3t: The newly added token is one that symbolises wealth and the game's central theme of money, not travel or communication.
Q5709.L4t: The new Monopoly token is a bag of cash, the sack of money.
Q5709.L2f: Hasbro has never changed the Monopoly token lineup, and every token is still the one in the 1935 original.
Q5709.L3f: The latest token was chosen to represent international travel and the worldwide reach of the Monopoly brand.
Q5709.L4f: The newest Monopoly token is the one shaped like the planet Earth.

Q8468.L1t: Hypothesis testing compares a test statistic with a critical value or a significance level to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis.
Q8468.L2t: A two-sided test splits the significance level between both tails of the distribution, so each tail's critical region is smaller than in a one-sided test.
Q8468.L3t: In the original situation the test statistic was extreme enough that even after doubling the one-sided p-value for a two-sided test, it still falls below the significance level.
Q8468.L4t: The two-sided test still gives enough evidence against the null hypothesis, so the null is rejected.
Q8468.L2f: A two-sided test always uses the same single critical value as a one-sided test, so changing the alternative never alters the rejection region.
Q8468.L3f: In a hypothesis test the alternative hypothesis is the one that gets rejected whenever the test statistic is significant.
Q8468.L4f: The conclusion is that the alternative hypothesis is the one rejected.

Q8505.L1t: Naturalism and positivism are two long-standing schools of thought in the philosophy of law and international law.
Q8505.L2t: Natural law thinking goes back to thinkers such as Grotius, while legal positivism became dominant in the nineteenth century.
Q8505.L3t: Natural law theory grounds law in objective, universal moral principles discoverable by reason, whereas positivism grounds law in what states have actually enacted or consented to.
Q8505.L4t: Naturalism rests on universal, objective rules, while positivism rests on a coherent legal order created by states according to their own interests and wishes.
Q8505.L2f: Positivism in international law was first articulated in the Middle Ages, before any notion of state sovereignty existed.
Q8505.L3f: Naturalism developed and is mainly championed by scholars outside Europe, while positivism was developed exclusively by European jurists as a regional doctrine.
Q8505.L4f: The main difference is geographic: naturalism comes from outside Europe, and positivism is a European-centred theory.
